paragraphs.text: Welcome to Lesson 22 of the Everyday English Speaking Course.

Situation number one – saying hello and goodbye.
There are many different ways to say hello in English and some of them require a different
If the other person says one of these – hello, hi, hi there, hey, hiya, howdy, you can respond
In these phrases, hello is the most formal and hey, hiya and howdy are the least formal.
Instead of hello, the other person might also say a phrase like this.
If everything is good, then you can reply.
Alright, if everything is not good, then you can reply.
If you give one of the not good responses, be prepared to say why you are feeling bad, because

I just got back from a business trip.
I've been studying a lot lately.
I'm looking forward to the dance festival this weekend.
There are also a number of ways to say goodbye in English.
Here are some formal or informal ways.
Use these expressions if you will definitely see the other person later.
Again, those phrases can be used in both formal and informal situations.
We also have some ways to say goodbye that are only used in informal situations.
Talking about your country and job.
It's common for people you meet to ask about your country and job.
If someone asks, where are you from?
I'm originally from Russia, but now I live in Italy.
I was born in Russia, but I grew up in France.
To ask about your profession, native English speakers don't usually ask, what is your job?
Instead, we say, what do you do?
Or, what do you do for a living?
The correct way to answer this question is to say, I'm and then the name of your profession.
I'm between jobs at the moment.
Click on the link in the lesson text for more ways to answer questions about where you work.
There will probably be a few moments in your English conversations when you don't understand
If you didn't hear what the other person said, you can say, pardon?
Sorry, I didn't hear what you said.
Could you speak a little slower, please?
If you understood the basics, but you want to get more information or details, you can say,
This asks the other person to restate their idea in different words, or in more detail.
If you want to check if the other person understood you, then you can say, do you know
Situation number four, showing interest in the conversation.
When the other person is talking for a long time or telling a story, it's good to show
that you are interested in what they are saying.
We'll learn more of these small responses to conversations in a later lesson.
Finally, here are two tips to keep a conversation going.
Try to ask questions that start with who, what, when, where, why, and how.
Try to avoid yes or no questions.
Also, in each of your answers, give one or two details that will help continue the conversation.
You don't need to talk for a long time.
For example, if someone asks you, what did you think of the New York City bus tour?
Instead, you can say, yes, my favorite part was visiting the Empire State Building.
That encourages the other person to make a comment about the tour, or ask you another question,
Situation number five, ending a conversation.
It's a good idea to say, anyway, it was nice talking to you, or, anyway, it was nice chatting
This signals to the other person that you want to bring the conversation to a close.
Then complete the sentence with one of these options.
Anyway, it was nice talking to you, but I should get going.
Anyway, it was nice chatting with you, but I've got to head out.
Anyway, it was nice talking to you, but I've got to run.
All of these options mean that you need to leave.
Now you know typical expressions for handling social conversations in English.
There's no quiz today, so you can relax a little bit.
Tomorrow, you'll learn different ways to talk about likes, dislikes, and preferences.
